There is, of course, an irony to telling Tuchel to sort out his defence. Isn’t this what we wanted? England were limp…

quietus.title: His Last Major Stand: Songs In The Key Of Life Turns 50
quietus.description: David Stubbs unpicks Stevie Wonder's transition from a technological pioneer to a musically conservative finger wagger of the highest order, and wonders just what might have been Ten years ago this Summer as part of the BST Festival at Hyde Park, Stevie Wonder performed his classic double album Songs In The Key Of Life in its entirety. Shameless nostalgia notwithstanding, it was almost certainly a stormer. Wonder has never lost his sheer, infectious, convulsive ability to entertain, to wrench every last, fat droplet of emotion out of any song he turns his voice to. He's 76 now – he was 26 when Songs In The Key Of Life was released, in 1976. At that point, he was absolutely on top of the...

quietus.title: There Must Be Some Kind of Way Out of Here: An Interview with Hang Linton
quietus.description: Ahead of their appearance at Decolonise Fest, fiercely DIY punk Hang Linton tells Emily Wilson about distrust of a gangster-infested music industry and the double-edged sword of building a social media fanbase Photo by Laura Lulika It’s easy to wonder if Hang Linton ever gets any sleep. The Leeds musician is a force of ambition and activity. They’ve spent the past few years gigging relentlessly, featuring on panel discussions, attending residences in Hanoi and Cambridge, writing, recording, and self-producing. On top of it all, they run their Instagram page like it’s the navy. Linton is a totally DIY, self-taught artist whose aim is to butt heads against the boundaries between genres, and…

quietus.title: Tiiva – This Could Be A Start
quietus.description: Tiiva This Could Be A Start UK producer's soundtrack to an imaginary video game delivers a maximalist hyper pop sucker punch blue fifty-nine/this could be a start by Tiiva Video game design and hyperpop share a clear sonic DNA, defined by maximalism, shape-shifting identities and non-linear structures. From the music genre’s inception, its most formative artists have embedded game tropes into their digital soundscapes. With This Could Be A Start, Lake District-based producer and game designer Tiiva delivers a compelling addition to this well-trodden collision of spaces. The result is a euphoric, emotionally resonant record, despite occasional forays into over-reverence toward the pop…

quietus.title: Living And Dying, Laughing And Crying: the Legacy of Cliff Burton
quietus.description: The undiminished, deep affection for Metallica’s late bassist Cliff Burton reveals a lot about the strength of fanhood in the implacable face of tragedy, says Joel McIver on the 40th anniversary of his death Cliff at his first soundcheck with Metallica at The Stone, San Francisco, 5 March 1983, by Brian Lew I spent six weeks in southern Sweden recently and encountered the spectre of Death in two significant locations. The first was at a rocky beach called Hovs Hallar, near the town of Ängelholm, where the late director Ingmar Bergman shot a couple of apocalyptic scenes from his 1957 film The Seventh Seal. If you know the famous opening scene, you’ll recall that the personification of Death…

quietus.title: Carrying the Fire: Cormac McCarthy’s The Road and the Tradition of Apocalypse
quietus.description: Cormac McCarthy's tenth novel was published 20 years ago. Auden Alsop revisits it and considers the inheritance of assured destruction and how this intersects with parenthood We all know that the world will end. All of this – everything you can see on and behind the screen on which you are reading this piece, and everything you can't – will be lost. We don't know how, when, or why. A nuclear (mis)fire, the eruption of one volcano or another, asteroid impact. When it happens, the how will not matter. Sometime in the ever-nearing future is when; there will be no why. Cormac McCarthy's novel The Road, which turns twenty today, is a simple story, told in ascetic prose, set during the after,...

quietus.title: Animals, Burns and Barns: Trav by Taylor Burns
quietus.description: Taylor Burns' novel Trav is savage and is boldly literary, finds Tristam Vivien Adams Travis Barnes is the protagonist. Taylor Burns is the author. It’s a bildungsroman. The names give it away. The names also resonate with the reading experience on many levels. Author’s name first: Burns. One can be scalded from encountering too cold or too hot a substance. Trav is an intense reading experience. Intense with neutral valence, for the book is by turns frosty and searing. Harrowing and life affirming. Exciting. Stimulating? yes. Pleasant? Joyful? on occasion. Such is life. Welcome to realism. The reading experience is oxymoronic: bleakness is rich and intricate; passion is at times doily…

The lineup has been put together by SQUARE's organisers, and its network of festival and events partners, such as Iceland Airwaves, MENT, Rewire, Nyege Nyege and Novas Frequências. The theme of next year's SQUARE will be Continuity, and this will explore "the projects that endure,…

quietus.description: The set at Knockdown Center formed part of the Detroit artist's 30th anniversary tour for his Live At The Liquid Room, Tokyo mix compilation Jeff Mills has released a new set recording via Apple Music, capturing a set that he played at New York's Knockdown Center in March of this year. The show, which was Mills play all-vinyl, formed part of his tour around the world in support of the 30th anniversary reissue of his classic Live At The Liquid Room, Tokyo mix compilation last year. The set was recorded in Spatial Audio using 14 microphones that Apple Music set up around Knockdown Center. It's been split into two parts, with the first part available for streaming now alongside a Ken Ishii…

aquariumdrunkard.title: Lee Ranaldo :: Guitar-Centric Film Soundtracks
aquariumdrunkard.description: As a member of Sonic Youth, Drift, and his many other musical detours, Lee Ranaldo has treated the guitar as a pure sound source, creating dynamic new expressions in rock & roll and the avant-garde alike. But Ranaldo's new project, a soundtrack to director Joris Postema’s "eco-doc" The System, presents a new side of Lee, that of a filmic composer. To commemorate the album's release, Ranaldo sent over notes about nine other guitar-centric soundtracks that serve as conceptual inspirations for The System.

aquariumdrunkard.title: The Aquarium Drunkard Guide to Across the Horizon
aquariumdrunkard.description: What, exactly, is Across the Horizon? It could be accurately described as a podcast, a radio show, an imprint or even a genre; it’s also resulted in a host of compelling collaborations and a series of songs that push at the boundaries of what could be considered ambient music. "It’s like watching a musical community grow in real time," says Bob Holmes. Here’s a look at 10 standout songs from Across the Horizon thus far — music that demonstrates the breadth of the series as a whole.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Dungen :: Vidrig Vår
aquariumdrunkard.description: On the veteran Swedish outfit's most pared down and elegant affair, Vidrig Vår showcases Dungen still operating on a psychedelic wavelength not found elsewhere. Built around bandleader Gustav Ejste's panoramic piano progressions, the ballad-centric record flows with the weightless springtime atmosphere of the band's organically cinematic orbit.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Asher White :: Love Aggregates
aquariumdrunkard.description: Asher White goes maximalist on Love Aggregates , building heavy doses of orchestral power pop from her bedroom. A fragmentary heartbreak album touching on dysphoria, precarious labor, Jerry Garcia, Citi Bikes, and Flatbush in the snow, it transforms intimate falsettos, arpeggiating guitars, and toy piano melodies into a luminous, redemptive vision of love.

aquariumdrunkard.title: Those Were the Days of Miracle and Wonder :: Paul Simon’s Graceland at 40
aquariumdrunkard.description: Paul Simon’s 1986 album Graceland exists in this weird state, an album that eternally evokes 1986, but always sounds so different from other albums of its era. It’s an collection that’s self absorbed, but also so relatable when the listener finds themselves hitting middle age. It brought world music to the forefront, but also presented a misleading picture. It’s a fascinating study in contrast and now, some 40 years later it’s an album we still can’t make up our minds about even as we listen to it for the hundredth time.

aquariumdrunkard.description: This week on the show, guitarist and psychotherapist Matt Baldwin, who is here to teach you How To Play Guitar. OK, not exactly. But Baldwin is the author of ⁠How To Play Guitar⁠, a series of zines that have been collected into a handsome book edition. If you’re just picking up the instrument, well, Baldwin isn’t writing about how to play a C chord or run scales. These aren’t “how to” guides so much as “why to” prompts, stressing intuition over technique, dismissal of music industry norms, and the imperative to hone a singular, personal philosophy regarding the instrument—think Captain Beefheart’s “Ten Commandments of Playing Guitar.” In this talk, we discuss his own guitar journey, the…
